A1.justification: Both PDFs describe SELFELICIT and provide readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices A–C. Retained material can be matched reliably despite expanded appendices and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original QA evaluations across six language models and four datasets, alongside attention analyses, robustness tests, and appendix ablations.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds attention measurements, strategy comparisons, an unanswerable-question experiment, and a threshold-related failure case.

M1.justification: Equations (1)–(4), Algorithm 1, and the prompting procedure retain the same attention aggregation, sentence selection, and highlighting method. The default remains the last 50% of layers with alpha = 0.5. Additional variants are evaluated as comparisons; dynamic threshold selection remains future work.

E1.justification: The four original datasets and existing distractor setting are retained. Appendix B.6 adds a HotpotQA scenario where some supplied contexts contain no supporting evidence, extending evaluation to answer rejection without introducing a new source corpus.

E2.justification: The original Table 1 comparators remain. Appendix B.7/Table 11 adds Filco, a trained context-filtering comparator, and crosses SELFELICIT/Filco evidence selection with highlighting/filtering. Table 9 also adds beginning- and end-attached evidence comparisons. These substantially expand the comparisons supporting the design.

E3.justification: Original validation splits, sample counts, model checkpoints, greedy decoding, and QA metrics remain unchanged. New protocols include replacing contexts for randomly selected 50% of HotpotQA samples and measuring rejection accuracy, plus averaging attention across all layers and heads before and after highlighting. These are additional experimental procedures, not reported revisions to the original evaluations.

E4.justification: New analyses test whether highlighting increases attention to evidence, whether evidence placement or filtering affects accuracy, and whether the method preserves rejection of unsupported questions. Appendix C.1 adds a failure case repaired by lowering the threshold. Original layer, threshold, token-versus-sentence, and distractor analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports run or seed counts, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The existing attention plots and point-estimate reporting are retained; the new randomized context-replacement experiment adds no seed or repeated-run information.

E6.justification: Original per-dataset Table 1 scores remain unchanged, but swapped average EM/F1 rankings are corrected: Llama3.1-8B Base changes from 4.75/4.38 to 4.38/4.75. Tables 7 and 9–11 add substantial results for attention, alternative strategies, Filco, and unsupported questions. In the new unanswerable setting, rejection accuracy is 91.25 for Base and 92.86 for SELFELICIT.

T1.justification: The mathematical definitions and attention-scoring equations are unchanged. Appendix C.2 adds qualitative reasoning about evidence use across layers, without introducing mathematical assumptions, propositions, derivations, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the central claims of training-free, efficient attention-based evidence highlighting that improves contextual QA. The conclusion retains the 5.0%–11.7% improvement claim. Revised grounding terminology and descriptions of additional analyses do not redefine the core contribution.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations concerning attention redistribution, information lost through filtering, incomplete evidence selection, and declining evidence attention in final layers. Its limitations replace the discussion of repeated input encoding with threshold selection and adaptation. The noise discussion also removes the unresolved TK% statement and emphasizes adaptive evidence selection.

D1.justification: Appendix A and new Table 5 disclose dataset-specific context sources and average/maximum token lengths, including use of the Llama-3.1 tokenizer for counting. Existing sample counts, model access references, implementation framework, segmentation details, decoding settings, and code link remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning around attention sorting, SnapKV, Filco, and DoLa. Section 5 explicitly distinguishes sentence-level evidence highlighting from document-level attention ranking and trained filtering, while Appendix C.2 connects findings to layer-wise factuality research. The bibliography and general-AI citations also expand considerably.

P1.justification: Most original prose and the main section hierarchy are retained. Editing concentrates on the introduction, robustness discussion, and limitations, with added acknowledgments and appendix subsections. Existing analyses and examples are largely preserved through renumbering.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands displayed evidence through new dataset-statistics, attention-change, strategy-comparison, and unanswerability tables, plus paired threshold-failure callouts. Existing figures remain, with several displays relocated. Original full-context Tables 7–8 become Tables 12–13 without changing their examples.

improvement.justification: v1 lacked direct measurements of highlighting's effect on attention, comparison with trained context filtering, and an explicit no-evidence test. v2 addresses these gaps and adds a concrete failure analysis, substantially strengthening validation and clarifying applicability. Ranking corrections also improve reporting accuracy. There are localized weaknesses: Appendix B.5 overstates the HotpotQA advantage of in-context highlighting despite Table 9 showing 69.8 for beginning-attached evidence versus 69.5 in-context, and the repeated-encoding limitation disappears. These shortcomings do not outweigh the stronger empirical support.
